Nothing really, its the first significant step in discovering additional exploits and launching non authorized software aka homebrew because ram can now be dumped. Most of your ordinary jailbreaks involve poking around inside the ram via some method that the hypervisor (software the decides what kind of access other pieces of software have to hardware or OS processes) either can't detect or can be blinded somehow then modifying the specific content of the piece of code in ram to do something it wasn't intended to do.

A common way to do this is to interrupt the CPU with a branch to an instruction that contains so many more instructions that whatever the CPU was doing before the interruption has to be put into a specific area of ram or internal CPU memory aka "stack" address, then you try to modify the original instruction so when the CPU finishes with the interruption branch it will read and execute your newly modified instruction which could itself point to more instructions giving you carte blanche to do whatever you want.

The trick is finding a way to do the interruption and instruction modifications in a way that the hypervisor can't catch and you won't crash the system. More elaborate jailbreaks involve tricking the hypervisor and OS processes into running emulating disc drives for piracy.

When placed in context with a console, all these things are actually true.

1) maintaining a PC requires a skill set not everyone has.

Maybe you do, but a lot of people still see it as a magic box they don't understand. When something goes wrong with a PC, they don't have the faintest idea about where to start. In fact, they don't really even want to know where to start. They're either relying heavily on friends to fix things, or they're paying ridiculous shop rates to have questionable people do the work.

2) Even though the total cost of ownership is lower (older games are often cheaper), up front it's often more expensive to get a gaming PC. It's hard for people who don't know hardware to understand what makes a good gaming PC.

I generally tell people that they can get in for as little as $500, but if they want a really good experience they should be prepared to spend closer to $1000. Can you build systems cheaper than $500? Sure. But it's going to be a pile of shit. I think the most damaging thing one can do when introducing someone to PC gaming is to encourage them to build/buy/use a box to play games on which causes them problems. Better to invest in quality in the first place, even if it sets you back a little more.

3) Ongoing upgrades

OK, it's less of an issue now than it was 5 years ago but there are still times when an upgrade is in order. Most people don't want to be bothered with the internals of their computer. While we know swapping out a video card is not that big a deal, regular people are scared to death of it. To them, it makes more sense to just buy a new system once the old one no longer meets their expectations. Consoles better fit this idea that electronics should be disposable. Consoles generally do not need upgrades since their specs are not a moving target.

PC gaming is awesome, but it's not without a learning curve, and it's not without its own caveats. Some people are better off with consoles, because it better suits the level of understanding those people are willing to achieve.
